metaTitle: Best Leaf Vacuums for Mulching in 2026
metaDescription: Six leaf vacuums compared on airflow, mulch ratio, impeller build and power source, so you can clear fall leaves with less bagging and less hauling.
expertTake: The EGO LV5000 is the best leaf vacuum for most big yards because of its 500 CFM airflow, six-blade metal impeller and 16:1 mulching, though the battery is extra. The Heywork corded unit is the value pick for small lots. Skip a leaf vacuum if your trees are few and your lawn is small, because a rake and a mulching mower do the same work.
introParagraphs: A leaf vacuum is a blower that runs backwards, pulling leaves through a fan that shreds them into a bag. It sounds simple, but the specs on the box describe air moving, not leaves shrinking, and wet leaves and sticks defeat many machines that look strong on paper.

This guide explains how airflow, air speed and mulch ratio work together, why the impeller material and power source matter, and how to match a machine to your yard. The quick picks are above, and the reviews below show which one suits which job.

buyingCriteria.explanation: CFM is the volume of air a machine moves and MPH is how fast it moves at the nozzle. For vacuuming leaves, CFM is the number that draws them into the tube, while MPH matters for blasting debris from hard surfaces. The EGO LV5000 lists 500 CFM at 210 MPH, the BLACK+DECKER lists 400 CFM at 250 MPH and the Heywork lists 450 CFM at 158 MPH. Read the pair together rather than chasing one big number.

A ratio such as 16:1 means a stated number of bags of leaves become one bag of shredded leaves. Manufacturers measure it under favorable conditions, usually with dry leaves. The WORX WG509 lists 18:1, the EGO 16:1, the Heywork and MZK 15:1, and the cordless WORX WG583 only 12:1. A lower ratio means more trips to the compost pile.

The impeller is the fan that chops leaves, and plastic fans crack on acorns and sticks while metal ones survive. The EGO LV5000 uses a six-blade metal impeller, and that is a major reason for its price. Any machine can lose a blade to a rock. Pick metal if your trees drop hard seeds or twigs, and inspect the impeller each season.

Corded machines give unlimited runtime and often a better mulch ratio, but the cord limits where you can work. Battery tools give freedom, but runtime is the limit: the MZK lists up to 30 minutes and the EGO up to 90 minutes on low with a 6.0 Ah pack. The EGO does not include its battery, while the MZK and WORX WG583 do. Match the tool to your yard size and the number of batteries you own.

A larger bag means fewer trips to empty, but a full bag gets heavy. The WORX WG509 has a 42 L bag, the EGO and Heywork 40 L, and the BLACK+DECKER uses a backpack bag. Look for a zipper that opens easily and wheels that support the vacuum tube. The Heywork weighs 5.5 lb, which matters over an hour.

Wet leaves are the cause of most jams, because they pack into the tube and gum the impeller. Anti-jam features like the MZK's internal suction tube and the EGO's wide, metal-tipped opening help. In practice, let the leaves dry for a day before vacuuming, because no machine here is built for soaking wet mats. Always switch off and unplug before clearing a clog.

specDecoder.meaning: Cubic feet per minute is the volume of air the blower moves at the nozzle. In vacuum mode, airflow through the tube is what carries leaves to the impeller, so higher CFM generally means better pickup.
specDecoder.watchFor: CFM is measured at the nozzle in blower mode, with no tube restrictions, so vacuum performance will be lower. The MZK's 700 CFM claim is far higher than the EGO's 500 CFM on a bigger battery.

specDecoder.meaning: MPH is how fast the air leaves the nozzle. It lets a blower lift stuck leaves off hard ground but matters less for vacuuming.
specDecoder.watchFor: Some makers quote MPH with a tapered nozzle only. The EGO's 210 MPH needs its nozzle attached.

specDecoder.meaning: The ratio is the factor by which the volume of leaves is reduced after shredding. A higher ratio means fewer bags to dispose of.
specDecoder.watchFor: Ratios are manufacturer estimates on dry leaves. Real reduction varies with leaf type and moisture.

specDecoder.meaning: A brushless motor uses electronic commutation, so there are no carbon brushes to wear out. That generally gives better efficiency and runtime on a battery tool.
specDecoder.watchFor: Brushless does not guarantee strong airflow. Look at CFM and battery voltage as well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow and air speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated CFM and MPH across the lineup, from the 340 CFM WORX WG583 to the 700 CFM claim on the MZK, and noted which numbers apply only in blower mode.

howWeEvaluated.title: Mulching and impeller build
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed mulch ratios from 12:1 on the WG583 to 18:1 on the WG509 and looked at whether the impeller is metal, as on the EGO LV5000.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and runtime
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered corded versus battery operation, battery voltage and the stated runtime, such as 30 minutes on the MZK and 90 minutes on low on the EGO.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling and clog resistance
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed weight, bag size, backpack versus side bag layouts and anti-jam features, such as the MZK's internal tube and the EGO's metal-tipped intake.

howToChoose.intro: The size of your yard and the number of trees decide whether you need corded or cordless.

rows: Quarter acre with a few trees

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: Unlimited runtime and generally a better mulch ratio per dollar. The WORX WG509, Heywork and BLACK+DECKER are corded, so you work within cord reach.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: No cord to snag and the freedom to roam. The EGO LV5000, MZK and WORX WG583 are cordless, but runtime is limited by the battery.

howToChoose.note: Pick corded for small and mid-size lawns. Choose cordless for scattered beds and big lots.

howToChoose.subheading: For Oak and Maple Trees Specifically

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A metal impeller, a wide intake and a decent mulch ratio. Acorns and sticks break plastic fans, and maple leaves clump when wet.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The EGO LV5000 fits best, with its metal six-blade impeller and wide metal-tipped tube. The WORX WG509 is the corded alternative with the highest mulch ratio.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You have large lots and trees that drop hard debris, which points to the EGO LV5000. You also want a longer warranty on a premium tool.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your yard is small and near an outlet, where the Heywork or WORX WG509 is enough. You can also use a rake for beds and save battery costs.

maintenance.why: Leaf residue and sap build on the blades. A clean impeller prevents jams and keeps the fan balanced.
Chips or bends cause vibration and poor shredding. Replace worn blades before they damage the housing.

maintenance.task: Empty and shake out the bag
maintenance.why: Damp leaves left in the bag mold and clog the mesh. A clean bag improves airflow.
Battery contacts corrode and cords crack in storage. Test the tool before the busy fall weeks.
Moisture damages electronics and batteries. Keep batteries at moderate temperatures.

faq.q: Is a corded or cordless leaf vacuum better?
faq.a: Corded tools offer unlimited runtime and strong mulching, while cordless tools offer freedom. If you work near an outlet, corded is cheaper and more powerful. For a big lot, choose cordless with spare batteries.

The least expensive corded machines cover small lots. Mid-tier tools add better mulch ratios and larger bags, and premium cordless tools add metal impellers and warranties. Include the cost of batteries if they are sold separately, as with the EGO.

faq.q: What does the mulch ratio mean?
faq.a: It describes how much the volume of leaves shrinks after shredding. A 16:1 ratio means about sixteen bags of leaves become one. Real results depend on leaf type and dryness.
You can, but wet leaves clog tubes and impellers on any machine. Let them dry for a day if possible. Anti-jam designs help but do not remove the problem.
Higher CFM usually means better pickup, but only when it is measured honestly. Claims are made in blower mode with no tube restrictions. Compare the CFM and MPH together.

faq.q: Is a leaf vacuum worth it over a rake?
faq.a: For small yards, no, because a rake is cheaper and quiet. Large yards with many trees save hours and bags with a vacuum. The mulched leaves also work as compost.

products.name: EGO Power+ LV5000 Cordless Leaf Vacuum and Mulcher

specList.label: Airflow
specList.value: Up to 500 CFM, 210 MPH with nozzle

specList.label: Runtime
specList.value: Up to 90 minutes on low, 6.0 Ah

products.description:
The EGO LV5000 is the best all-rounder because the parts that wear out in a leaf vacuum are built for it. A six-blade metal impeller does the shredding, which matters because acorns, sticks and wet leaf mats destroy plastic fans. The vacuum tube has a metal-tipped, wide opening to reduce clogging, and the whole tool carries an IPX5 weather rating and a five-year tool warranty.

Airflow is the headline: up to 500 CFM and 210 MPH with the tapered nozzle, the highest verified blower airflow in this lineup. It mulches at 16:1, which is better than the cordless WORX at 12:1 and in line with the corded picks. The catch is that the battery and charger are not included, so the real entry cost is the LV5000 plus a 56V battery, and if you already own EGO tools you can reuse them. A 6.0 Ah battery is listed for up to 90 minutes on low, and that figure drops fast on high.

In use, the variable speed dial and soft-grip auxiliary handle make long jobs manageable. Check the bag zipper and the clog access, because wet leaves are what stop all leaf vacuums, and keep the intake clear of sticks thicker than a thumb.
products.bestFor: Homeowners with a half-acre or more of trees who already own or want to buy into the EGO battery platform.
pros: Metal six-blade impeller resists acorns and sticks
Highest airflow of the verified specs in this lineup
Five-year tool warranty and a weather-resistant IPX5 build
Variable speed dial and a wide metal-tipped vacuum intake
cons: Battery and charger are sold separately, raising entry cost
Listed 90 minute runtime applies only on low speed

products.name: Heywork 3-in-1 Corded Leaf Vacuum Mulcher, 450 CFM
products.description:
The Heywork is the lightest machine in this lineup at 5.5 pounds, and it is corded, so there is no battery to charge, replace or run down halfway through a pile. Its 450 CFM airflow beats the WORX WG509 at 350 CFM on paper, while its 158 MPH air speed is the lowest here, which tells you it is tuned for moving volume of dry leaves rather than blasting damp debris off a driveway. The 15:1 mulch ratio is comparable to the EGO's 16:1.

A nested internal tube and a square connector with a secure buckle are meant to reduce debris buildup and keep the bag attached. Wheels support the tube in vacuum mode on flat ground, and a shoulder strap handles carrying. The practical limits are the cord and the unproven brand: you are tied to an outlet or an extension cord, and the long-term durability of a newer listing is an early signal rather than a track record.

Use a heavy-gauge extension cord rated for the amperage and keep it clear of the intake, because a snagged cord is the most common corded-tool mishap. Dry leaves mulch well, and wet ones clump in any machine at this size. Empty the bag before it fills past two-thirds so that airflow stays high.
products.bestFor: Smaller lots near an outlet where light weight and no battery matter more than reach.
pros: Lightest machine in this lineup at about 5.5 pounds
Corded power means no battery to buy, charge or run flat
Support wheels and shoulder strap ease long sessions
450 CFM airflow is strong for a light corded tool like this
cons: Cord limits range and needs a decent extension cable
Lowest air speed here at 158 MPH, weaker on wet debris
Newer listing with a short long-term durability record so far

products.name: WORX Trivac WG509 Corded 3-in-1 Leaf Vacuum
products.description:
The WORX Trivac WG509 is the best-known corded 3-in-1 for a reason: it combines a 12 amp motor, a shredding impeller and a 42 liter collection bag with the highest claimed mulch ratio in this guide, 18:1. That means roughly eighteen bags of leaves reduced to one, though ratios depend on the leaf type and dryness. A flip of a lever switches between blowing and vacuum modes without tools.

Its 350 CFM and 210 MPH put it behind the EGO's 500 CFM and the Heywork's 450 CFM in volume, while it matches the cordless WORX WG583 at 340 CFM. The reason to pick it over the cordless version is continuous power for a long session and a better mulch ratio. The trade is the cord, so range is limited to what you can reach, and a corded machine is heavier than the cordless tools to hold and move.

Since the WORX line has accessories sold for larger jobs, check compatibility with the listed leaf accessories before buying. Variable speed lets you throttle down around flower beds, which prevents blasting mulch off the garden. As with any leaf vacuum, empty it frequently, keep the impeller clear and unplug the machine before clearing a jam.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who mulch heavily and want a reliable corded tool with the best claimed reduction ratio.
pros: Highest claimed mulch ratio in this lineup at 18:1
Continuous corded power suits long cleanup sessions well
Large 42 L bag and a tool-free vacuum to blower mode switch
Variable speed lets you throttle around garden beds
cons: Corded range limits where you can work without a long cable
Lower airflow on paper than the EGO and Heywork models
Heavier to hold for long than the lightest corded pick here

products.name: MZK 40V Cordless Leaf Vacuum Mulcher, 700 CFM Claimed
products.description:
This is a cordless machine that ships with two 4.0 Ah batteries, so it works the day it arrives. The brushless motor, four speeds and a 10 second Turbo burst are designed for moving wet debris. The claimed 700 CFM and 180 MPH are very high for a 40V tool, and you should read them as a peak figure rather than a sustained number, since the EGO at 56V lists 500 CFM.

The anti-jam design uses an internal suction tube that prevents clogging at the joints, and a quick-access cleaning gate helps clear obstructions fast. The 15:1 mulch ratio matches the Heywork, falls behind the 18:1 WORX WG509 and beats the 12:1 cordless WORX. Wheels with adjustable height take weight off your arms. The listing states up to 30 minutes of continuous runtime, which is the real limit of the cordless approach and shorter than the EGO's 90 minutes on low.

A 40V platform from a lesser-known brand means batteries and parts will be harder to find if the tool outlives its warranty. Charge both batteries before starting, and swap them rather than run flat.
products.bestFor: Cordless shoppers with a mid-size yard who want two batteries and a charger included in the box.
pros: Two batteries included so it works straight out of the box
Anti-jam internal tube and a quick-access cleaning gate
Four speeds plus a short Turbo burst for wet debris
Adjustable-height wheels carry part of the tool's weight
cons: Listed 30 minutes of runtime is short for a big yard
700 CFM claim is a peak figure, not a sustained one
Parts and battery support are less proven than the big brands

products.badge: Best for the WORX Battery Platform
products.name: WORX WG583 40V Cordless 3-in-1 Leaf Vacuum with Two Batteries
products.description:
The WG583 is the cordless sibling of the WG509 and shares its 210 MPH air speed. Cordless freedom is the point: you can clear the back garden without an extension cord, and the wheeled vacuum tube takes some of the weight in vacuum mode. A brushless motor and two 4.0 Ah batteries with a dual charger are included, which makes the kit complete.

The cost of cordless is mulch performance and runtime. Its 12:1 mulch ratio is the lowest in this guide, versus 18:1 on the WG509 and 16:1 on the EGO, so you will fill bags faster. The 340 CFM is similar to the corded WG509's 350 CFM, but the battery limits how long it can sustain high speed. The PowerShare system lets you share batteries across other WORX 20V, 40V and 80V tools, which is the main reason to choose this one if you own them.

Because it uses a two-speed control, use the low setting for sweeping around beds and high for heavy piles, to stretch the pack. If you do not already use the WORX battery family, the corded WG509 will be the better mulcher for the same job.
products.bestFor: Owners of other WORX cordless tools who want a leaf vacuum that shares their batteries.
pros: Cordless freedom with two batteries and a dual charger
PowerShare batteries work across WORX 20V and 40V tools
Wheeled vacuum tube helps carry weight in vacuum mode
Brushless motor extends runtime over a brushed design
cons: Lowest mulch ratio in this lineup at 12:1, so more bags fill
Battery runtime limits long sessions at high speed

products.name: BLACK+DECKER BEBL7000 Corded 3-in-1 Backpack Leaf Vacuum
products.description:
This corded model changes the layout: instead of a bag hanging off the side, the bag is a backpack that you wear while vacuuming. That moves weight from your wrist to your shoulders, which makes a long session easier on your arms and shoulders. The zipper-free bag has a wide opening so emptying is quick, and the Flexi-Tube improves maneuverability around beds and shrubs.

It offers 250 MPH and 400 CFM with a PowerBoost button for extra power on demand. That 250 MPH is the highest air speed here and well above the Heywork's 158 MPH, and the 400 CFM sits between the WORX WG509 and the Heywork. The listing does not state a mulch ratio, so unlike the WORX at 18:1 you do not have a number to rely on. The backpack bag has up to twice the capacity of a typical side bag, which is helpful on large lawns.

Being corded, it shares the extension cord limit of the other corded picks, and a backpack bag filled with damp leaves gets heavy fast. Empty it before it is full, wear it with the waist strap snug and inspect the impeller for wear after each season.
products.bestFor: Larger lawns where carrying a full bag on your back is easier than a bag hanging from the tool.
